Written by Christos Giannakoulas and Manolis Zachariadis
The mechanism that started Greenwood is no longer in the game
Years before Greenwood existed, while working on another project called "Monstrocity", we designed a dice-based worker-placement system. The dice did not belong to individual players. Instead, they were placed in shared action areas, where their values affected both the strength of an action and which dice would return to the players. "Monstrocity" never found its way to publication, despite years of work, but the mechanism stayed with us.
When we began designing Greenwood, we had two starting points: We wanted to build a eurogame around this system, and we wanted to set it in a fantasy world of druids, ancient forests, and a mysterious evil slowly revealing itself. The first versions included a map, construction, elements of area control, and the dice mechanism at their center. The game gradually developed into two main parts.
During the first, players used their dice to recruit characters and prepare their fellowship and during the second, they activated those characters, used their abilities, and sent them into the forest.
First physical play-testing of the first prototype of Greenwood.

As the game developed, however, the second part kept becoming more interesting, while the mechanism that had inspired the project became increasingly complicated. We worked on its mathematics, experimented with different ways to refresh the dice, and introduced solutions for situations that were not working as intended. We were able to resolve these issues, yet the game itself was becoming harder to navigate. The decisions were meant to be complex; the procedures around them had become cumbersome. Eventually, we had to admit that the mechanism had become an elaborate preparation for the more interesting part of the game.
So we removed it.
It was a difficult decision. The mechanism was the reason Greenwood existed in the first place, but removing it was also consistent with the way we had gradually learned to design together.
We like to begin a design by defining a framework and placing restrictions on ourselves. A defined space gives us a specific problem to solve and pushes us toward solutions we might otherwise never consider. We sometimes describe it as working inside a box in order to think outside it.
A restriction can be useful even if the game eventually grows beyond it.
When the Card Became Everything
For Greenwood, removing the dice mechanism gave us the space to reconsider what the game could actually become. This left us in a strange situation. We had taken away the system around which Greenwood had originally been designed, while the parts that had gradually become more interesting were still there.
Players were assembling a fellowship of characters and deciding how to use them. A character could offer an individual ability or be sent into the forest to perform a broader action. We needed a new framework that could connect these elements and give the game a clearer identity. Some of the cards were already serving more than one purpose, so we decided to push that idea much further: What if the card could be almost everything?
Cards could become Companions, pay costs, or represent different resources depending on how they were used. The exact functions changed repeatedly during development, but we tried to solve each new problem through the cards first.
Early Companion Card that could be used for its abilty, as a potion, as a beast ally, for its key-icon or as currency for the game.

This was when we began describing Greenwood as a euro-inspired card game.
We wanted the planning, development, and interconnected decisions of a eurogame, with most of that experience carried by cards. We even removed the map and central board, which belonged to an earlier version of the design. As we worked with this approach, we found that the multiple uses of a card became interesting when they competed with one another. Playing a card as a Companion meant losing whatever else that card could have provided, while using it as a resource meant giving up the possibility of adding that Companion to your fellowship. That tension gradually became one of the foundations of the game.
The next challenge was asymmetry.
We wanted every player to represent a different clan, with each clan interacting with the common card system in its own way. One might turn cards into potions, another use them to create magical energy, while another would introduce a different mechanism altogether. A private faction deck for each player would have been the obvious structure. Instead, we built a single shared deck. Every game began with a set of common cards. Each participating clan then contributed its own group of cards, and all of them were shuffied together.
This became one of the defining ideas of Greenwood.
The deck scaled naturally with the number of players, and only the mechanisms belonging to the participating clans entered that particular game. More importantly, choosing a clan changed the card environment for everyone at the table.
Your clan’s cards entered the shared deck, where other players could recruit and use them. Each combi-nation of clans therefore created a different version of Greenwood for the whole table. We wanted the clans to remain distinct while continually crossing into one another’s systems. Your choice of clan sha-ped your own possibilities, but it also changed what everyone else could find and use. The shared deck created an obvious challenge. Another player might gain access to your clan’s cards before you did, so we needed a reliable way for each player to retain a connection to their clan’s central idea.
This eventually became the Primal Spirit: a permanent representative of your clan that gave you access to its core mechanism, while the clan cards allowed that mechanism to spread through the shared deck. The Spy mechanism developed from the same idea. Players could make limited use of Companions in another fellowship, giving them a reason to watch what the others were building and how they were using it. This made the other fellowships relevant to your own plans as well.
By this point, Greenwood had found a much clearer direction. Its identity came from the tension between the different uses of the cards, the way each clan changed the shared system, and the opportu-nities that emerged from the choices of the other players. After extensive playtesting and balancing, we believed Greenwood had gained a distinct identity.
It was time to find out whether a publisher would see the same potential in it.
Finding the Right Fit
Publishers have their own identities. Before pitching Greenwood, we spent time learning more about Feuerland, their catalog, and the kind of games they were interested in. We also contacted them to better understand what they were looking for. This helped us feel that Greenwood could genuinely be a good fit for them.
We eventually pitched the complete game to Feuerland, and their response was positive enough to continue exploring it, including a later session through Tabletop Simulator. They also identified several areas that they felt needed more work. Our approach was to look beyond the proposed solution and understand the experience behind it: what caused hesitation, what felt unclear, or where the game was not delivering as strongly as intended.
Tabletop Simulator version of Greenwood, that was played with the Feuerland Team for the first time.

We returned to Greenwood, worked on those areas, and prepared a revised version. After seeing the revision, Feuerland decided to move forward with the game. By the following year, we were ready to sign the contract.
At that point, Greenwood was a complete game, with its core systems, structure, asymmetry, and identity already in place. We expected further development as part of the publication process.
What followed became a much deeper collaboration than we had anticipated.
From a Euro-Inspired Card Game to a Card-Based Eurogame.
Feuerland was already very positive about the core of Greenwood. At the same time, the game now had to become not only a Goblins on Board design, but also a Feuerland game. We admired Feuerland partly because their catalog had such a recognizable character. Their games reflected a clear unders-tanding of the kind of experience the company wanted to offer, and this was one of the reasons we had approached them in the first place.
Looking back, we sometimes describe the version we presented as a euro-inspired card game, while the direction in which the collaboration took it was closer to a card-based eurogame. This was never a phrase Feuerland used with us, and there was no formal decision to transform the game from one category into another. It is simply our way of understanding the changes now. Our version was built around the idea that the cards should carry almost everything. A card used as a potion, for example, represented the potion itself, while Forest actions were performed through cards and player boards rather than movement on a central map.
During development, some of these abstract functions gradually acquired a physical presence. A card could be discarded and replaced by an actual potion token. Forest actions became connected to move-ment through an actual forest. The map had returned.
The Map of Greenwood by night.

This was slightly amusing to us, because we had removed a map years earlier when we decided that the cards should be everything. But it was not really a return to the old version of Greenwood. The new map was not carrying the old area-control system. It was giving physical form to actions that already belonged to the newer game. This became one of the ways in which our original restriction evolved during development. Some ideas became clearer and more satisfying when they were represented phy-sically, while the multifunctional use of cards remained at the heart of the game. Other additions went further.
The Feuerland team introduced the idea of the vessel that eventually became the Submarine, where rescued creatures are placed as polyomino tiles. Rescuing a creature now also meant considering its shape, the remaining space in the Submarine, and the bonuses its placement could unlock. The spatial puzzle became closely connected to one of the main actions of the game and eventually to its story as well.
The theme was developing at the same time. Our original story placed the players in the role of druidic clans protecting an ancient forest from a hidden evil and its minions. We liked the setting and had developed the identities of the clans alongsi-de their mechanisms. Feuerland wanted to develop the world further with Jan Cronauer, and we were curious to see where another perspective could take what we had created. The result surprised us in the best possible way.
In the new setting, the druids had become the High Circle, exploiting mystical creatures behind the carefully maintained image of a natural paradise. The players became Primal Spirits leading independent fellowships into Greenwood at night to free those creatures. One of the simplest mechanical phrases in the prototype changed from fight a minion to rescue a creature.
It was a small change in wording with much larger consequences for the way the game felt. The creatures became the reason for entering Greenwood, while the Submarine naturally became the place where they were hidden and carried to safety. The Knowledge players collected also gained a clearer role: perceiving traps, seeing through illusions, and breaking the hexes holding the creatures captive.
We had started with a theme we already liked and ended with one that preserved much of its atmo-sphere while changing its perspective. The clans, forest, magic, and hidden darkness remained, but their relationships had evolved along with the game.
This kind of exchange became characteristic of the collaboration. We often approached the same prob-lem from different directions. An idea proposed by one side would be tested, changed, and sometimes return as something neither side had originally suggested. Some of the most productive moments came from these third solutions. The Feuerland team became active participants in the development, building on the systems, structure, and identity already at the heart of Greenwood.
For a while, we felt that development was moving toward its final stages. Then, after observing new players at another convention, the Feuerland team came back to us with a simple question. What is the most interesting and distinctive part of Greenwood?
Our answer was the asymmetry – especially the way each participating clan changed the shared deck and introduced possibilities that could be accessed by everyone. Then came the more difficult question. Was that part of the game as strong in play as it sounded when we described it?
The honest answer was no.
The system worked. The clans affected one another and created different combinations, and players could feel some of that difference. Yet the asymmetry was still less prominent in the actual experience than the idea itself suggested. We had spent a great deal of time making the asymmetry work. We now needed to make it matter.
One More Year
Strengthening the asymmetry reached far beyond a few clan abilities. It affected cards, balance, visu-al language, theme, and graphic design, at a point when Greenwood was already moving through the schedules of development, illustration, and production.
At the next SPIEL Essen, the Feuerland team told us that the release would move to the following year. They believed the extra time could make Greenwood significantly better. Naturally, we wanted to see Greenwood published, but we were completely on board with the decision. After years of changing mecha-nisms, components, and even major parts of the theme whenever we felt the game benefited from it, rushing the final stage simply to preserve a release date would have felt inconsistent with the way we had developed it. We also appreciated Feuerland’s willingness to change their schedule and give the game that time. And there was plenty to do with it.
One area we focused on was complexity. Some of Greenwood’s weight came from the decisions we wanted players to face; some had accumulated through smaller rules and exceptions introduced during years of development. We went back through the game looking for places where those rules could be removed, combined, or replaced by cleaner solutions, while continuing to strengthen the clans and the differences between them.
By then, we had also learned how easily long-term familiarity can hide friction. Procedures become familiar, exceptions are easy to remember, and small awkward moments can gradually become almost invisible to people who have lived with a prototype for years. Feuerland therefore organized a three-day playtesting event devoted to Greenwood, with around twenty to twenty-five gamers, most of whom had never played it before.
For three days, the cycle was almost continuous: Play. Observe. Discuss. Change. Play again.
That speed was one of the most useful parts of the event. An issue seen in one game could be discussed immediately, adjusted, and tested again while the previous session was still fresh. With several tables playing independently, we could also see which patterns repeated across different groups and which were simply unusual results from a single game. The event gave us a great deal of information about balance, pacing, repetitive strategies, unnecessary rules, and the clans themselves.
It also gave us something much less technical. People continued playing.
Most of these players had no personal connection to us or to the history of Greenwood. Yet after finishing a long game, many of them chose to sit down and play again. They discussed clans, tried different combinations, and kept going until everyone was exhausted. For us, that became the emotional highlight of the development process.
After years of looking at Greenwood through mechanisms, numbers, and successive versions, we were watching unfamiliar players engage with the game simply because they wanted to.
But their enthusiasm did not hide the remaining problems. In fact, the same three days showed us very clearly where more work was still needed. We left the event with a much sharper direction for the final stage of development. Over the following months, we continued refining the clans, reducing unnecessary rules, correcting problematic patterns, and working with the rest of the team as the game moved toward production. The extra year gave us the time to do that properly.
As Greenwood Reaches the Players
A board game can be tested hundreds of times before publication, by designers, development teams, long-term playtesters, and people encountering it for the first time. Then the game reaches the public, and the game enters a very different environment.
Players will open the box, learn the rules, make decisions we cannot observe and experience the systems without knowing the history behind them. They do not see the mechanisms we removed, the versions that failed, or the discussions that led to a particular rule. They only experience the Greenwood that finally reached them. For years, the game existed mostly as a series of questions in front of us. Does this clan feel different enough? Is this rule necessary? Does this component communicate the idea more clearly? Does the game deliver the experience its strongest ideas seem to promise?
Soon, players will see the results of these questions. And maybe come up with their own. They will combine different clans, build their fellowships, explore Greenwood, rescue its creatures, and discover interactions and approaches that we may never have considered.
Looking back, the path to the final game was far from straightforward. We removed the mechanism that had started the project, rebuilt its framework, allowed its physical form and theme to evolve, strengthened its asymmetry, and eventually accepted an additional year of development. Much of that happened through a collaboration in which we and the Feuerland team often approached the same problems differently. Testing those different perspectives, rather than simply choosing one over the other, became an important part of how Greenwood evolved.

Now the mechanics, artwork, graphic design, rules, and world have finally come together. The prototype we carried with us for years has become a finished product shaped by many more people, than the two names printed beside “Designers”. We are excited, proud, and naturally a little nervous.
Because, in a sense, the final and largest playtest begins when the game reaches the public. Then the game belongs to its players. (We hope Greenwood brings you the same joy we had, while devolping it)
A Thank You
We would like to thank the entire Feuerland team for their trust in us and in Greenwood, and for the care, ideas, and work they brought to the game throughout its development. We are also deeply grateful to everyone who playtested Greenwood over the years and helped us shape the game that will finally reach the table.
About the Designers
Christos Giannakoulas and Manolis Zachariadis design board games together as Goblins on Board. They are the designers of Greenwood, published by Feuerland Spiele.
